items.title: How I Make CRAZY Designs with Deepseek for $1
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll show you Stageshow, the new MIT-licensed skill from Benji Taylor that gives your agent his whole 7-step process for building product demos, from the placement and the story to filming its own demo and passing a gate before it hands anything over. Then I'll show you why it gets really good when you combine it with Hallmark for the page and Emil Kowalski's skills for the motion polish, and why I run all of them on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with DeepSeek's own harness, dsh, inside PandaCode for very little money. After that, I'll set the whole thing up step by step, including the new Skills manager in PandaCode with its safety check and per-project switches. Then I'll give it a real job, a landing page and hero demo for my small expenses app Halves, and walk through every check it fails and fixes along the way. Finally, I'll be honest about the downsides and tell you what I think.

--

items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, you know how the product demo on most landing pages is either a flat screenshot that nobody looks at or an animated thing that an AI agent made where everything slides in at once. There is fake text in every row and the cursor wanders around for no reason. You can tell a model made it in about 2 seconds. Benji Taylor, who is the head of design at X, just put out a skill that goes after exactly that. It is called stage a show, and it gives your agent his whole process for building product demos, not just a list of rules. And I think it is one of the best skills I have seen this year. But the part that I actually want to show you today is what happens when you combine it with a couple of the other design skills that I have covered like Hallmark and Emil Kowalsski skills and then run all of them on DeepSeek V41 Flash with Deepseek's own harness inside Pandaode because each skill fixes a different part of the page and together the results get kind of crazy for very little money. I'll also show you how to set the whole thing up with the skills manager in the latest Panda Code because that takes care of the most annoying part of using skills. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about what Stage of Show actually is. It's on GitHub under Benji Taylor/skills. It's MIT licensed and it's at version 1.1 right now. It builds faux product UI, which means a simplified copy of one screen of your app, either as a still image or as a short animation with a draw-in cursor. These are illustrations, not screen recordings. When the script says click, it draws the cursor pressing, and the scene changes because the script tells it to. The skill starts with one idea. The demo should read as a real product simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion should have a cause. And then it lists the five ways AI demos go wrong. Too much, where every row has real text and numbers. Wireframe, which is two gray blobs and a button. Boxed, which is a whole window shrunk into a card. Flat, where every object has the same weight, so the eye has nowhere to land. and bland, which is a gray window with a cursor, whatever the brief said. If you have asked an agent for a hero animation before, you have probably seen all five. Now, the reason this works better than a long prompt is that it's a process and the agent has to go through it in order. It starts with the placement. Is it a still or an animation? Where does it sit on the page? And how big is it going to be? It designs at the size that people will actually see it. and it builds a separate phone version at 358 pixels wide, which is a redesign and not just a squeeze. Then it looks at your product. If your app's code is in the project, it reads your colors, your fonts, and your corner radius and maps them to its own kit. So the demo looks like your app and not like a template. Then comes the story. One action, 3 to five beats, and a payoff in 10 to 16 seconds. And there's a rule that I really like here, which is that no cursor move is allowed unless you can explain why it's there. Then it starts from a real example. The repo has 71 examples, including more than 40 gold ones that Benji built himself, like an AI chat, a table edit, a drag to reorder, and a payout flow. The agent picks the closest one, films it, and copies its structure instead of starting from a blank file. Then the screen itself, where it only gets three to seven real words. Everything else is placeholder bars. That is a big part of why these demos don't look generated because the words only go where the story is. Then the motion with curved cursor paths, parts that move instead of swapping, and a loop that ends where it began, so you never see it restart. And the last step is the one that makes it really different. The agent films its own demo frame by frame with a script, checks every beat in a contact sheet, and since version 1.1, there is a gate that it has to pass before it can hand the demo over. If the gate prints even one problem, it goes back and fixes it. Then it writes a rehearsal.mmd file which says which example it started from, what it changed, and what it didn't check. And Benji is pretty honest about the limit here. The check catches mistakes, but it can't tell you if the idea is boring. You still have to decide that. Now, here's the thing. Stage a show only builds the demo. It doesn't build the page around it. And that's where the other skills come in. Hallmark from Nutlope and Together AI builds the page. It has 50 themes where each theme is a material like a paper, a type, and a pallet. and it doesn't tell the model what the page contains. It deals three of them for your brief, builds the page in the one that fits, and then it checks the result in a real browser and fails the build when the page has the usual AI tells like the tracked capital labels over every heading or a purple gradient. Then Emil Kowalsski's skills handle the motion polish. Emil made sonner involve and his skills know things like why an enter animation should use ease out and not ease in and why a button that you click 50 times a day should not have a 400 millisecond transition. His review animation skill goes through every transition in your code and flags those and it only runs when you call it with its slash command. So the agent never runs it on its own. So the way I see it, Hallmark decides how the page looks. Stage a show builds the product moment inside it and Emil's skills make every motion on the page feel right. They don't fight each other because each one owns a different part of the job. One thing I would not do is stack hallmark and taste skill together. Both of them pick the look of the page. So you just get two creative directors arguing. Pick one of them and then add stage a show and Emil's skills on top. Now why deepseek for this? These skills are not cheap to run. Stage a show reads its references, films an example, builds the demo, films it again, and loops until the gate passes. That's a lot of turns. and every turn reads the same long skill files. Again, most of those tokens are cash reads, and that's exactly where Deepseek V4.1 Flash is the cheapest. At off peak hours, it's 15 cents per million input tokens, 60 cents per million output tokens, and 310 of 1 cent per million for cash hits. Sonnet 5.5 is $2 in and $10 out. And you get the model inside the harness that it was trained for. The Deepseek harness, which is called DSH, is Deepseek's own agent loop. Pandode just starts it in the background and talks to it. So you get Deepseek's agent with Pandaodes interface on top which means the file changes the terminal the git panel and the cost of each run. Now let's set it up. First get the latest P code. Go to the Pandode GitHub page. Open the releases and download the newest build for your system or just update it from inside the app. I'm on version 0.31219 here. Next install the Deepseek Carus. Open your terminal and run npm install-g at deepseeek-ai/DSH. Pandaode finds it on its own. Then go to settings, agents, providers, and paste your DeepSseek API key into the DeepSc card or just set the DEPCK API_key environment variable. Now the skills, go to settings, tools, skills. This page lists every skill that is installed for any agent on your computer. And this is also where you add new ones. Click add skill and in the source box, type Benji Taylor/skills and click find skills. It reads the repo directly and finds stage of show with its description. Under agents, tick deepseek. You can tick clawed code and codeex as well if you use them. Then pick where it goes. All projects puts it in every agent's home folder. Or you can pick just one project. And for design skills, I like keeping them in the project. Then click install. Now do the same for the other two. Type nut/hallmark, find it, tick deepseek, and install it into the same project. Then type in milowalski/sklls. This repo has 20 skills now. So you get a list and you can tick only the ones you want. I took the main design engineering skill and review animations and left the rest. Panda code also runs a safety check on every skill that you add. It scans the files for things like secrets or a script piped straight into your shell. And if it finds something, it quarantines that skill until you look at it. Stage a show ships scripts and a whole React kit. So it's really nice that this happens on its own. And now all of them are in the list, each with its own switch. You can turn a skill off for one project or for all projects. And it applies from the next turn without uninstalling anything. For Deep Seek, Panda Code can only ask the agent not to use a skill that is off. And the page tells you that with a may still load note. So if you really don't want a skill to load, uninstall it. Last step, start a new task in that project. Open the model picker, choose DeepSeek, pick V4.1 Flash, and set the thinking effort to max. Don't skip that because thinking makes a huge difference on this model. Now, let's give it a real job. I have a small app here called Halves. It's a shared expenses app for flatmates where you add a bill and it splits it between everyone. The app is done, but it has no landing page. So, I'll type use Hallmark to build a landing page for this app and then use stage a show to make the hero demo from the real app screens. Hallmark goes first. It reads the app, deals its three themes, picks the one that fits a small, friendly money app, and builds the page. Then it runs its check in the browser, and the first full run fails on a few things, like a placeholder that's too low on contrast and spacing that's off its own scale. It fixes them, runs the check again, and now it passes. Then stage a show takes over, and you can see it following the process. It reads the app's own tokens, so the demo gets the same green, the same font, and the same rounded rows as the real app. It writes the story down before any code. Someone adds a 42lb grocery bill. It splits three ways. Each flatmate's balance rolls to the new number and the payoff is the settle up button lighting up. Then it picks the table edit example as the closest gold. Films it and copies its structure. Then it films its own demo with the gate on and it catches things that you would never notice by eye, like one digit that pops in instead of rolling and the numbers jumping a little when the font loads. It fixes both films again at the desktop and the phone width. And this time it gets rehearsal passed. Then it writes raarsalt saying that it started from table edit swapped in the heavs look and did not check it in Safari. Then I run /re animations on the page. It flags the toast that appears when you add a bill which uses a plain ease and slides in by animating its margin and a 220 millisecond hover on the main button with one line on why each one feels wrong. I tell it to fix both and it changes the toast to ease out on a transform and the button to 160 milliseconds. And this is the result. The hero has the real Hal screen simplified with the bill being added, the split and the balances rolling and it loops without you ever seeing it restart. The page around it doesn't look like a template and every animation on it feels quick and calm. There's also the phone version which is a proper layout and not just a smaller copy. And all of this ran on DeepS v41 flash. In Panda Code, you can see every command it ran, every file it touched, and the token usage for the whole run. It's a long run, but most of those tokens are cash reads. So, the whole page with the demo and the polish pass came in well under a dollar. Now, let me be fair here. These skills make the model slow stage of show films, checks, and films again. And that is the point, but it's not something that you run for a quick mockup. Plan for a long run. Deepseek V41 flash is also not the best model at taste. The skills carry most of the design decisions, but the model still makes choices. And on a bigger brief, a model like Opus 5.5 will make better ones. Your code also goes to Deepseek servers. So check that first for private work. And the pricing is real off- peak pricing. So run the long jobs at off peak hours when the price is half. And again, stage a show's own check can tell you that something is broken, but it can't tell you that the idea is boring. That part is still on you. So what do I think? I think stage a show is one of the best skills out there right now because it gives the agent a real process and not just rules and the combination is where it gets really good. Hallmark gives you a page that doesn't look generated. Stage a show puts a real product moment in it. Emil's skills make all the motion feel right.
